title: Functional Completeness of Connectives
quickIdea: A set of connectives is functionally complete when every truth function can be built from it. NAND alone and NOR alone are complete; {and, or} is not, because it cannot express negation.
remember: A set S of connectives is functionally complete when every Boolean function is expressible as a formula using only connectives from S.
{not, and}, {not, or}, {not, implies}, {NAND} and {NOR} are each functionally complete.
{and, or} and {and, or, implies, iff} are not complete: every formula they build is monotone, so negation is out of reach.
{xor} and {xor, and} are not complete: every formula they build is 0-preserving, so negation is again out of reach.
NAND builds negation as p NAND p, and then AND as not (p NAND q). NOR builds negation as p NOR p, and OR as not (p NOR q).
Post's criterion: a single connective is complete only if it is not 0-preserving, not 1-preserving, not monotone, not self-dual and not affine.

example.prompt: Build not p and p and q using only NAND.
example.work: p NAND p is not (p and p) = not p. Then p NAND q is not (p and q), so (p NAND q) NAND (p NAND q) = not not (p and q) = p and q.
example.answer: not p = p NAND p; p and q = (p NAND q) NAND (p NAND q)

gateAngle: GATE 2015 Set 1 Q.39 gives f(X,Y,Z) = X'YZ + XY' + Y'Z' and g(X,Y,Z) = X'YZ + X'YZ' + XY and asks which singleton is complete. Setting Y = X in f gives f(X,X,Z) = X'Z', which is NOR, so {f} is complete; g preserves 0 and 1, so it cannot be.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is {xor, and} functionally complete?
variations.why: Both connectives return false when every input is false, so every formula built from them is 0-preserving: at all-false input the value is false. Negation must map false to true, so it cannot be expressed.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is {and, or} not functionally complete?
variations.answer: Every formula built from and and or is monotone, so negation cannot be expressed
variations.why: Raising a variable from false to true can never turn a monotone formula from true to false. Negation does exactly that, so it lies outside the set.

trap.what: Assuming any set of connectives is complete, or checking completeness by trying a few examples.
trap.why: Completeness is a claim about all Boolean functions. Either exhibit a known complete set (such as NAND) built from the candidate, or use an invariant such as 0-preservation that rules it out.
trap.counterexample: {and, or} looks rich - it has two connectives and builds all monotone functions - yet not p is not monotone, so the set fails.

check.question: Express not p using NOR only.
check.explanation: p NOR p is not (p or p) = not p. NOR is complete, so everything else can then be built from it.
